prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its development to the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a measurement-capability discovery of the kind I trust: a simple, original idea (magic-wavelength trapping, Katori) that removes the Stark and motional shifts while keeping the statistical power of many atoms, followed by a demonstrated gain of orders of magnitude over microwave standards (Ye and JILA). The performance has been reproduced by several independent laboratories, the comparison and systematics work is thorough, and the claimed accuracy is not a single-group result that depends on trusting one team. The credit is unusually clean: two names, two distinct and complementary roles, both on every colleague's proposed list. It also has the widest support in the room: all eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three, and two placed it first. As Chair I weigh that breadth, but I would not support it on breadth alone; the physics (relativistic geodesy, tests of constants and dark-sector couplings, and the route to redefining the second) will last.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty against the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland, ion control): a skeptic can say this is the next increment in a metrology lineage that has already been recognised twice. The second concern is whether this is a discovery or a refinement of an existing technique, and whether the committee should wait until the redefinition of the second is actually adopted. Finally, ion clocks and Yb or Al+ groups made parallel advances, so the 'highest accuracy' claim is one the leading groups trade back and forth. I judge these as real but not disqualifying, since the lattice concept is a distinct invention. I am also not a specialist in atomic physics, so I would want expert reviewer input on the relative priority of Katori, Ye and the earlier lattice-clock proposals.

responses.point: IceCube (B035) is the discovery in which nature supplied the clue: a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux, then TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068, opening neutrino astronomy and attacking the century-old cosmic-ray origin problem.
responses.response: I agree with Ulf on the science, and I ranked B035 first myself, so this is not a disagreement about merit. My hesitation is about timing and credit. The diffuse flux is solid, but source identification still rests on a handful of objects, and the instrument credit sits with a large collaboration, so naming Halzen and Spiering would leave out the DUMAND and AMANDA lineage and the collaboration leadership. As Chair I cannot ignore that only Ulf and I placed it in the top eight. I keep it as my first alternative and think it can be a strong candidate in a few years once source catalogues firm up.

responses.point: Olle asks whether lattice clocks are engineering-level metrology or a fundamental physics discovery, and notes the overlap with the Hall and Haensch and Wineland recognition, while favouring Kane, Mele and Molenkamp (B048) as a new quantum state of matter.
responses.response: The engineering-versus-discovery question is a fair one and it is my main reservation as well. My answer is that the magic-wavelength idea is an invention with a clear physical mechanism, and the resulting 10^-18 measurements are what open new science, such as redshift tests across millimetres. That is closer to the instrument-led window I value than to routine improvement. On B048 I defer to the condensed-matter members on the physics, but I share Olle's own worry that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang omission and the 3D topological insulator work make the credit fragile, which is a practical argument for the cleaner two-name configuration.

responses.point: Stefan ranks the lattice clock first as a direct step in measurement capability, with 10^-18 uncertainty and a path to redefining the second, and keeps B001 experimental.
responses.response: I largely agree and this is why I move B013 to the top of my own configuration. I would add one qualification to his case: the overlap with the frequency-comb and ion-clock prizes means the citation should be written around the lattice concept and its 10^-18 realisation, not around clocks in general, so that the committee does not look like it is recognising metrology a third time without a new idea. I also agree with him that the experimental trio in B001 is the right way to treat the optical lattice simulation candidate.

responses.point: Bernhard puts Aharonov-Bohm and Berry phase (B034) first for its universal geometric structure, and ranks lattice clocks sixth, asking whether to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I take the conceptual weight of B034 seriously, but I disagree on its fit as a prize now. It rests on priority questions (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam), Bohm cannot share, and as Bernhard himself says it lacks one decisive experiment, whereas the clock result is quantitative and independently reproduced. On waiting for the redefinition: the ordering of the new second is a policy step, while the underlying physics is already established and confirmed by comparison across laboratories, so I do not think the committee needs to hold back for it.

responses.point: Goran ranks circuit QED (B008) first as the architecture of superconducting processors, but notes that Wallraff is missing from the credited names and declares a conflict of interest.
responses.response: I appreciate the disclosure. The missing experimentalist (Wallraff) is a problem I cannot solve with the credited names, which weakens B008 as a three-person prize. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits also makes a second circuit prize so soon hard to defend. I would not exclude it permanently, but I do not put it in my preferred configuration or among my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a lattice-clock prize as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes
Whether expert reviewers would add or substitute another contributor (for example Ludlow, Lemke or the Yb and Al+ groups) beside Katori and Ye
Whether the committee wants to wait for the adoption of a new definition of the second
Atomic physics is outside my own expertise, so my view of relative priority in the clock lineage is second-hand
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the lattice-clock candidate. My own collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, XL-Calibur) are in astroparticle and gamma-ray work, not atomic clocks, though IceCube (B035), my alternative, is in my broader field and I would flag a possible proximity there, with no known personal tie to Halzen or Spiering.
